The duduk bass is a variant of the Armenian duduk, an aerophone, Hornbostel–Sachs 422.111. It is built with a cylindrical body of apricot wood, seven fingerholes at the front and a thumbhole at the back, and a broad double reed. It sounds when the breath sets the reed and the air in the tube vibrating, and half-holing gives the semitones. Armenian players often play in pairs, one carrying the melody and the other a drone, using circular breathing to hold the long note. It appears in the music of Armenia, the Caucasus, the Middle East and the Balkans, and is used in film scores.
杜德克低音管為 duduk 變體，源自亞美尼亞，屬氣鳴樂器。duduk 至少五世: The duduk bass is a variant of the duduk, which comes from Armenia and is an aerophone. The duduk existed at least by the fifth century; Armenian musicologists put forward evidence for the twelfth century BC and hold that it was already used in royal music in the first century BC, while other sources tie the history of duduk music to the reign of Tigran the Great. Its variants are spread across the Caucasus, the Middle East and the Balkans, and it is close to the balaban and the mey. Playing developed a duet form and the half-hole technique for semitones. In 2005 Armenian duduk music was proclaimed, and in 2008 inscribed, on the UNESCO intangible heritage list; later it became widely known through film scores.
